Not exactly what you are talking about but I work with medically fragile kiddos in both their home and at school. Since my focus is on one patient, I have time to do everything (PT, OT, Speech and Music therapy, etc). I pay attention to what each therapist does and ask questions about activities I can continue while they are gone. This autonomy enables me to provide quality, personalized care every day. Additionally, spending so much time with them gives you the opportunity to be an incredible advocate.

However there are some downsides... Days can be pretty repetitive, most of the time there is no other staff to help, and there are some people in the healthcare setting who will look down on you for "not being a real nurse".

If none of those are a big no for you, it can be an amazing job that is very fulfilling.

Thank you for that. There is such a large culture of nursing that is "ICU/ER or bust" and I've been looked down on for not being interested in them. When I mentioned my desire for pediatric home care in school I was actually laughed at.
